en: The Chapter on King Aśoka’s Undertaking of the Vows of Renunciation in the Teaching of the Sugata (with additional verses):
Then, Great King Aśoka, desiring once more to hear well-spoken words, [requested:]...
Having bowed to the ascetic Upagupta with palms joined in reverence, he spoke thus:
"Venerable sir, I wish to hear further of the majestic power of that Teacher of the World, the Lord of Munis; it behoves you to explain it."
Having heard this prayer made by the king, that wise Arhat ascetic addressed the lord of men and, looking upon him, spoke thus:
Now listen with focused attention; I shall explain it exactly as it was taught by my Guru, for the sake of increasing your merit.
Thus it was in the great city of Mathurā:
there lived a merchant named Sādhubhoga, a man of great means who possessed an abundance of all kinds of wealth.
His wife was named Priyaṃvadā, excellent, virtuous, with limbs as beautiful as Subhadrā, lovely like Rati, and possessing a form resembling Śrī.
To her was born a daughter with three limbs and a deformed body;
seeing that girl, the mother’s hopes were frustrated.
Janaka, too, having gazed upon that girl Triyantrikā,
stood with his heart pierced by shame, intent on sighing.
Then that merchant Janaka, having summoned many skilled and discerning non-Buddhist practitioners who were experts in omens, suddenly showed them the girl.
Seeing the infant bound by three fetters, that heretic, who was skilled in interpreting signs,
announced before the merchant, "This child is inauspicious."
Having heard that, the merchant Janaka stood with his mind agitated by fear and sorrow;
his soul tormented by the fires of affection and grief, his senses were utterly bewildered.
Having seen her and having heard what was uttered by that heretic, that virtuous wife became tormented by the fires of affection and grief, her heart deeply distressed.
At that very moment, that woman of great merit, an ascetic renowned for her mastery of all branches of knowledge, arrived there at the house of the merchant.
Seeing her approaching, the merchant rose up suddenly;
having greeted her with respect, he seated her upon a pure seat.
Then the merchant Sādhubhoga, having joyfully honored that female wanderer, fed her, and fully satisfied her, spoke as follows.
"A daughter named Bhadrikā has been born to me as my own child; she possesses three mechanical devices.
I wish to give her to you; you ought to consider this."
Having thus announced this, the merchant took his own daughter,
placed her before him, and spoke while presenting much wealth.
"O noble lady, this girl has been intended by me for you;
therefore, having accepted her, she should be nurtured by you as if she were your own daughter."
"You are bereft of sons and daughters, husbandless, and free from worldly distractions;
therefore, you must protect this child as if she were your own daughter."
Having thus announced this, the merchant joyfully gave his daughter, along with her nurse and accompanied by much wealth, to her, and spoke to her once more as follows.
When she has grown up, she will become your slave;
therefore, as long as she is still a child, she must always be protected by you.
Therefore, O noble-minded one, having initiated them into your own dharma, cause them to practice it;
and likewise, teach all the scriptures in their proper sequence.
Having spoken thus, the father, having mentally offered his daughter— adorned with garments and ornaments—
to that female ascetic, gave her to her with joy.
Having accepted that which was offered along with the nurse and attendants,
and having bestowed auspicious blessings upon him, Śrī then departed.
Having gone there to her own hermitage, she, being filled with joy, protected and suddenly nourished that girl along with her nurse as if she were her own daughter.
Thus being nurtured, she grew day by day;
with her faculties fully developed, she became lovely and enchanting to all.
Then, having been ordained according to the prescribed rite by that instructress,
she assumed the vows of an ascetic and lived wearing saffron robes.
Then that maiden Sumati learned all the scripts;
thereafter, she studied all the treatises in due order.

Having thus studied and mastered the furthest limits of all branches of knowledge, that wise woman became known by the name Mahādhīḥ; because of her excellent intelligence, she was called Triyantrikā.
Gradually, through the power of her own dharma and with the exhaustion of her former sins, that wise woman, whose limbs had been crooked, became as tall as a śāla tree.
Having mastered the sixty-four arts and attained proficiency in the study of the Vedas,
she shone forth, striking terror into the minds of all disputants.
All the learned disputants were utterly unable to defeat her;
she alone, having completely vanquished all opposing speakers, shone forth in splendor.
The fragrance of her fame spread in every direction; hearing of that noble-mindedness, everyone was struck with great wonder.
Then, a learned brahmin named Vidyākara, a man of honor who had mastered all the Vedāntas, arrived there from the south.
Having wrapped his side with a copper plate, he, uplifted in spirit,
entered that city joyfully while holding a blazing torch.
"He who desires to engage in debate with me here—toward him I shall approach," thought the conceited one and proceeded joyfully. (Svp 33)
Seeing him approaching, the great multitude of people from Mathurā addressed that brahmin and all spoke thus:
"O virtuous one, do not come here; hold this blazing torch!
That female ascetic who is virtuous, wise, and chaste—she is present."
Having heard what they said, Vidyākara, who was exceedingly proud, approached the Māthurikas and spoke to them with arrogance: Svp_36 //
"Which wise female wanderer is there residing here?
I wish to see her; you ought to show her to me."
Having heard what he said, all those great men looked at that brahmin and spoke thus in order to question him: [Svp 38]
"O virtuous one, if you wish to hold a conversation with her,
we shall show you that beloved, wise, and discerning woman."
Having heard all that was spoken by everyone, that brahmin, filled with joy and looking at all those people standing before him, spoke thus:
"O sirs, I am eager to hold a discussion with her;
therefore, bring her here and show her before me. (Svp 41)
Having heard what was thus related by him, those people said, "So be it," and having gone quickly to that hermitage, they approached that ascetic.
Seeing them seated there, that female mendicant joyfully asked them, "For what purpose have you come?"
Having heard that, all those people, bowing with palms joined in joy, beheld her of great intelligence and spoke thus to the women of Mathurā: Svp_44 //
There was a certain learned brahmin here, an expert in all the scriptures,
a wise man who had reached the further shore of Vedānta, who had arrived from the south.
If you wish to engage in debate with him,
then proclaim your own virtues in the midst of the assembly of all the world.
If you are able, O proud lady, engage in debate with that wise man;
for if you are defeated by him, we too shall become an object of ridicule.
Having heard what they said, that wise female wanderer replied:
"Very well, I do indeed wish to hold a debate with that brahmin."
"I shall display my virtues in the midst of the entire assembly of the world"—
hearing this proclaimed by her, everyone was filled with wonder.
They all reported this entire account before the king;
having heard it, the king [acted] exactly as they had spoken.
"Act in such a manner," he said to those people;
and having obtained his permission, all those people were filled with joy.
Having addressed those people and related this event, they spoke as follows:
"Together with this highly wise female wanderer..."
"A certain learned brahmin desires to engage in a dialogue;
those who wish to hear it and to understand its specific significance [should come]."
"Let everyone assemble there in the city on the seventh day from now," thus the king commanded, as they proclaimed it everywhere.
"Having sounded the bell, urge on the virtuous people!
Hearing those words spoken, all the good people were filled with joy.
There, all of them, filled with joy, acted exactly as commanded by the king; having rung their bells loudly, they brought delight to all the worlds.
Having thus made their vow and sounded the proclamation from the bells,
all the virtuous people residing in Mathurā heard it.
Desiring to hear and witness that dispute, they flocked together; then the proud Vidyākara thought thus within his mind: Svp_57 //
Thinking, "What kind of knowledge does that wise female wanderer possess? he remained there in his seat, observing the virtuous female wanderer.
Having gone to that hermitage to see [her], he asked the people there:
"Who is that wise female wanderer, and where does she reside?"
"Having summoned her, show her to me quickly.
Hearing this spoken, those who were stationed nearby [responded].
Having addressed that virtuous female wanderer, they spoke thus:
"O noble lady, a learned brahmin desires to see you."
"Having addressed her, may you show her with respect.
Hearing what was said by him, that female wanderer was filled with joy.
Having addressed that learned man,
he approached the beautiful female wanderer, who was charming, delightful, and exceedingly handsome, standing before him.
Having gazed at him for a very long time, her heart was set ablaze by the fire of passion;
and that female ascetic, too, beheld that handsome brahmin.
Their minds agitated by passion, they gazed intently at one another;
then, by the turn of fate, the fire of passion flared up between the two of them.
Because of that, their hearts were drawn toward one another and they became filled with affection;
then that lovely young brahmin, his senses agitated by passion, [fell in love].
Beholding that lovely, youthful, and beautiful woman in private, he said:
"O blessed lady of auspicious limbs, my mind, upon seeing you—"
The fire of passion blazes up to burn that;
O auspicious lady, if you have compassion for this wise Brahmin, you ought to extinguish it.
"Behold that with clear vision, comfort me, and rejoice!
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, that female wanderer also—
With her heart turbid with sensual passion, she remained as if utterly deluded;
and seeing her thus bewildered in mind, that brahmin also [fell under the spell].
Embracing her, gazing at her, and comforting her, he spoke thus:
"O blessed lady, if you have affection and a friendly mind toward me."
Having heard the words I have spoken, gladden your heart, O Sumati,
regarding that which you wish to debate with me.
I too am willing to engage in debate with you;
therefore, if you have affection for me, listen to these words of benefit.
"Having concentrated his mind upon that, he ought to perform it thoroughly.
Hearing what was thus said, the highly intelligent one became afflicted with desire.
Beholding Vidyākara, she smiled and spoke thus:
"O best of the twice-born, O one of great wisdom, it is exactly as you have instructed."
"I wish to do so; let it be declared that this is the truth"—having heard this declaration made by her, he was filled with joy.
With a smiling face, he who was overwhelmed by the old age of the god of love said to her:
"If this is done regarding Rāma, then there shall be a union for us two."
"Having made a mutual agreement and having established ourselves in secrecy, let us live and enjoy ourselves happily for as long as we live."
Thus, indeed, we two shall converse there in the midst of the assembly;
whoever is the victor in this dispute, his pride shall be destroyed.
"Having taken refuge and entered into discipleship, one should always follow [the teacher];
having made this realization and having witnessed it before a great assembly—
There, in the midst of the entire assembly, we shall debate with one another;
if I defeat you, O woman, then you will not be censured in the world.
"What wonder is there that a fool is defeated by a virtuous man?
But it will be said [as a marvel] if I am defeated there in the midst of the assembly by you, a woman."
Then I shall be censured on all sides in the world:
"Even a wise man, a twice-born brahmin, has been defeated by a mere young woman! (Svp 83)
"In this way, I, the most renowned author of knowledge, shall become an object of ridicule"—
thus did you then initiate that conversation between us there.
Not even a single word of reply should be given;
having thus been conquered by me, you shall then become my female disciple.
"Thus may there be a union between us, bringing great happiness for as long as we live.
Having heard what he said, she was inflamed by the passion of desire.
Having replied, "So be it," he dispelled the brahmin's distress.
Thus, having attained realization there through her, that brahmin, unobserved by the world, proceeded joyfully to his own home.
Then, on another day at dawn, the wise man, eager with desire,
went into the midst of a great assembly of people and, having addressed them, spoke thus:
"Gentlemen, today I wish to hold a discussion with that female wanderer; therefore, bring her here quickly."
Having heard what was spoken by him, all those great people agreed,
saying "So be it," and addressed that ascetic in this way:
That this brahmin, who is an expert in all the scriptures,
now desires to hold a conversation with you.
If you wish to debate with him,
then come and stand there in the midst of the assembly in that arena.
Having heard what was thus spoken, that female ascetic,
desiring him as her husband, joyfully took refuge upon the stage.
Vidyākara also arrived there at that assembly hall on the stage; having beheld Mahādhimukha, he approached him with a joyful mind.
There, having seen and heard those two seated together in the midst of the assembly on that stage, all those great people also took their seats.
Overcome with curiosity to see that, the Brahmins, the religious students,
and all the people led by the king gathered there.
Likewise, other virtuous people— artisans, merchants, subjects, and so forth—
all arrived there and took their places to witness that.
Beholding all those worlds seated together to see him,
that brahmin rose up and, looking at them with palms joined in reverence, spoke thus:
Sirs, please grant forgiveness for the childish restlessness we have displayed here out of our own excessive pride and arrogance.
If this woman is defeated by me in this debate, what wonder would the world say, that "a woman has been conquered by a man"? (Svp 99)
If I were defeated here in this dispute even by this woman, I would be censured by all, thinking, "A man has been defeated by a woman."
Therefore, having established an agreement here, I am eager to engage in debate;
may you virtuous ones, acting as impartial witnesses, deign to observe it.
If she should indeed be able to defeat me in this debate here, then,
having become her disciple, I shall forever be her follower.
If, having conquered her here, I should attain the glory of victory,
she would become my constant follower once she has entered the state of being my disciple.
Having thus made this earnest supplication to that virtuous female wanderer, the brahmin,
observing her and having asked about the matter of the prophecy, urged her on.
Addressing that response, the wise female wanderer defeated the brahmin and caused the members of the assembly to marvel.
Having heard that, all those people, their minds filled with wonder, said,
"This ascetic is wise," and returned to their respective dwellings.
Then on the following day, that female wanderer arrived there;
all those virtuous people also gathered together and took refuge in her.
Then that brahmin, seated there in the midst of the assembly,
looked at the female wanderer and questioned her about the meaning of the scriptures.
Having fully explained the meaning of that scripture, that wise young woman,
having defeated even that learned man, caused all the virtuous ones to rejoice.
And so, on the third day as well, that woman Sanmati likewise uttered examples of clear meaning in response to all the arts.
In this manner, on the fourth day, as well as on the fifth,
and likewise on the sixth day, she instructed him according to the truth.
Thus, on the arrival of the seventh day, that brahmin,
having entered into a formal agreement with her, proceeded to the arena.
With a mind agitated by shame, he spoke to the people with great eloquence:
"Even now, if I were defeated by her, would I not surely become her follower? (Svp 113)
"Thinking, 'She will thus conquer me every single day, how much more so on this one day,' she was nevertheless conquered by Sarasvatī, that woman who exists under the guise of Speech."
Having spoken thus, the lustful twice-born man questioned the woman of great intelligence, who was herself overcome by passion, about the Vedānta with bold words.
Thereupon, having been questioned, that virtuous and wise woman, recollecting her realization, was indeed unable to give even a brief reply.
Then that brahmin, seeing the great multitude gathered in the assembly hall,
with a face full of joy and serene composure, spoke thus with palms joined in reverence:
"Sirs, let it be seen who here attains the glory of victory;
having examined this, you ought to declare it, and certainly not otherwise."
Having heard that request, all those members of the assembly praised the treasury of knowledge, the one of great wisdom, and spoke thus:
"O wise one, you are the victor here; this ascetic has been defeated.
Therefore, let her be your disciple, following you for all time."
On that very same day, the Great Intellect was conquered by him;
"How can there be any doubt in this matter? they all asked in amazement.
Having heard this which was proclaimed by everyone, that brahmin, looking at the female wanderer with joy and smiling, spoke as follows:
O noble lady, come hither; having attained conformity with that which has been realized according to your own realization, practice the Dharma as my follower.
Having heard what was thus spoken, that female ascetic smiled;
with her face cast down, she stood as if her heart were struck by shame.
Then that brahmin, filled with joy, having given him a staff, an umbrella, and sandals,
and having suddenly taken leave of her and comforted her, spoke thus:
O blessed lady, it has been accomplished exactly as I desired;
therefore, come back with me and enjoy happiness together with joy.
Having heard what was thus said, that female wanderer then took her staff, sandals, and umbrella, and set out slowly.
Then that brahmin, having joyfully taken hold of the female wanderer,
went to his dwelling with the great enthusiasm of one victorious and glorious.
Taking up residence there, that wise man was greatly delighted;
enjoying himself with her as he desired, he lived happily.
While she was thus enjoying herself with that exceedingly passionate husband,
she became pregnant, just as a rain cloud becomes heavy with water during the monsoon.
Then, as her pregnancy gradually progressed, that woman became thin-limbed,
pale-complexioned, soft-spoken, and slow of gait.
Having been recognized as pregnant and being censured by the great multitude,
her heart shriveled with shame, and she spoke to that brahmin husband:
"O Master, please understand that since I am pregnant,
how could I conduct myself here now while being censured by the people?"
Therefore, my mind wishes to go and stay in another place;
if you desire to sport with me, go ahead, let us both depart.
Having heard what was thus related by her, that brahmin likewise desired to go to another region together with her. (135)
Then, having left Mathurā, the two of them went to the southern region;
wandering through the countryside there, they lived happily.
There, in that city called Śvetavalākā, the two of them, husband and wife, having gone there with joy and taken refuge for the night, dwelt there, being weary from their travels.
There, at the conclusion of nine months, at the appropriate time,
she gave birth to a handsome boy in the monastery located at the edge of the assembly hall of the world.
Beholding her son, who was as beautiful as gold,
that mother stood with a heart filled with wonder and her face bowed down in shame.
Janaka, too, having beheld him and thinking, "This one must indeed be wise," stood for a long time gazing at him with a heart full of joy.
Then Janaka, having personally performed the birth ceremony for him, reflected, "What name shall I give him? and spoke thus.
"Since this son of mine was born in the assembly hall (*sabhā*), let his name be celebrated everywhere as Sabhika, the Delighter."
Having thus related the matter according to the facts, the father gave that boy the well-known name Sabhika and sent him away.
Then that boy, well-nourished by both his mother and father,
grew up quickly with fully developed faculties, becoming a charming youth.
Then that wise gambler gradually learned the scripts;
having quickly mastered all the treatises, he attained the status of a great scholar.
Thus that wise victor over disputants, skilled in all branches of knowledge,
desired to defeat all those who were conceited about their learning.
Then, having obtained permission from his parents, that man of extreme pride went forth into homelessness; and, upholding the command of his teacher, he practiced the ascetic vows.
He whose mother was highly wise and whose father was likewise Vidyākara— therefore, the master of the gambling house was himself exceedingly proud and an expert in the sciences.
Then, desiring to conquer those who were proud, he went to a hermitage on the shore of the ocean to see the great sages and brahmins of discernment.
There, having defeated all the disputants who propounded various treatises and having attained victory, he wandered about filled with joy.
Then, having gone to another hermitage, that gambler observed;
having thus defeated all those who spoke [against him], he achieved victory.
Thus, having gone to the sixteen cities along with his assembly,
he conquered all the proponents of other doctrines and attained the glory of the fame of victory.
Then that master of the assembly, arrogant with the pride of mastery over all branches of knowledge, thought thus in his mind: "I shall defeat all the proponents of rival doctrines."
"He is the perfectly awakened one, possessed of great super-knowledge, the omniscient Arhat, the Lord of Munis;
he is now renowned everywhere as the conqueror of all disputants."
Therefore, O high-minded one, I shall go to that hermitage of that lord of sages, the teacher of the world, in order to understand his extraordinary wisdom.
The Buddha cannot be defeated; he is indeed a son of the kṣatriyas.
But at the time of battle, those kṣatriya heroes were averse to the sacred scriptures.
My father was the great sage Vidyākara, and my mother was herself one who had reached the further shore of the ocean of knowledge and who dispelled the pride of all disputants.
Having reflected thus, that keeper of the park went wandering to the Deer Park, the hermitage of the Victor in Vārāṇasī; having approached and beheld him, he drew near.
There he beheld that Lord of Munis seated in the assembly hall, surrounded by all the world, like the sun together with the full moon.
Seeing him, that man of great pride, his mind overcome with wonder,
stood with a gaping mouth, his senses motionless as he gazed.
Then, summoning his fortitude and abandoning pride and arrogance, he prostrated there with palms joined in reverence; gazing upon him, he approached.
Having approached there, he bowed at the lotus-feet of that Teacher, the Great Sage, and with palms joined in reverence, he took refuge in him.
There, with a deeply serene mind and palms joined in reverence, he stood before him and,
gazing upon that Fully Awakened One who possesses great supernormal knowledge, spoke thus:
O Blessed One, may you understand that for which I have come here;
it behoves you to fulfill that desire of my heart.
Having heard this request made by him, the Blessed One, the Jina,
looked toward that master of the gambling hall and, smiling, spoke as follows:
Listen, O virtuous and illustrious one, to that purpose for which you have come here;
I shall fulfill it for you—tell me what you desire.
Having heard what was thus commanded by the Lord of Munis, that keeper of the gambling house, filled with joy,
looked toward the Blessed One and spoke these words with palms joined in reverence:
"Blessed One, what knowledge have you attained and what is your vow, by which you are renowned as a Perfectly Awakened One? You ought to explain this."
Having heard that request, the Blessed One, who removes all pride and arrogance,
looked at Sabhika and gave this reply.
"Ask Uttara for the meaning of that matter, O Lord of the Assembly;
this man is ignorant before his disciples because he has grasped only a very small portion of the training."
Having heard these words of the Omniscient One, Sabhika Māṇika,
free from pride, smiled and, with palms joined in reverence, questioned the wise Uttara.
"You have been commanded by the Blessed One; therefore, instruct me for that purpose.
Requested thus out of discipline, he instructed him further for that purpose.
"How is it that you are ignorant, O presiding judge, you who are skilled in all branches of knowledge?
Listen attentively; I shall speak to you in brief."
Having undertaken the vow of the conduct of awakening and having attained supreme enlightenment,
he who awakens all is called a Perfectly Awakened One (saṃbuddha).

Having abandoned the home that is the abode of Māra, free from afflictions and with senses conquered, he who practices the vow of asceticism for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings; Svp_175 //
That Arhat monk, whose self is purified, who dwells in the four divine abodes,
who is a listener to the true Dharma— he is called the Saṅgha, that yogin, that ascetic.
Perceiving the world as a product of illusion, he who bears the welfare of himself and others, having taken up the vow of the conduct of awakening, practices for the benefit of the world.
That śramaṇa, possessing great supernormal knowledge, the refuge of the excellent qualities of Bhadraśrī,
is remembered as a bodhisattva, a mahāsattva, who upholds the meaning of all dharmas.
Having heard what was thus instructed by Uttara, that presiding judge,
filled with wonder, bowed to the wise Uttara and reported [the matter] again.
Who are the northern Brahmins, and who are the *snātakas*? How are they twice-born (*dvija*)?
How are the Vedic Brahmins (*vipra*), and how are those who are learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*)?
And how are they the knowers of the field (kṣetrajña)? And how are they celibate students (brahmacārin), seers (ṛṣi), wandering mendicants (parivrāja), sages (muni), and ascetics (tapasvin)?
How and by what means do ascetics and yogins [attain their state] through karma?
Having fully explained this karma, please awaken my mind.
When he had thus made his request, the mendicant monk Uttara looked at the master of the house and, smiling, spoke as follows:
And those pure-souled ascetics who rely on the dharma of non-violence,
who maintain the integrity of pure vows, and who are highly proficient in the practice of yoga;
Listen well with a concentrated mind to that which you wish to ask;
I shall explain it to you in brief for the complete satisfaction of your mind.
He who creates the universe— the self-existent Brahmā, the upholder of the Vedas, the Ordainer—
his sons are of pure conduct, characterized by sattva, and possessed of stainless senses.
Those who conduct themselves equally toward themselves and others, who dwell in the four divine abodes,
and who uphold the Vedas, the Dharma, and its meaning— they are remembered as true Brahmins.
Those who constantly bathe in sacred fords, who are pure in conduct and have conquered their senses,
and who practice the vow of celibacy without longing, are known as *snātakas*.
Those who are purified by their formative actions (*saṃskāra*), who practice the duties of the Vedas,
and who observe the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), are known as the twice-born (*dvija*).
Those who possess pure conduct and proper behavior, who accomplish the goals of the Vedas and Dharma,
and who are steadfast in their absorption in the practice of Brahman— they are remembered as Vaidikas.
Those who, having maintained the vow of Brahman, always move in what is auspicious and fulfill the purpose of the sixfold dharma— they are called "Brahmins" by the wise.
Those who are steadfast, great heroes, and dedicated to the welfare of all beings;
who uphold the auspicious meaning of the Vedas and are wise—they are remembered as true Vedic scholars (śrotriya).
He who understands the purification of that field which the Self takes as its support— the field of all the sense faculties— is called the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).
Those whose nature is loving-kindness and sympathetic joy, whose minds are moistened by compassion,
and who move among beings with equanimity for their welfare— blessed are those practitioners of the holy life!
Those who have desisted from the exertion of saṃsāra, who long for the bliss of nirvāṇa,
and who practice the vows of renunciation, are known as wandering mendicants (parivrājaka).
And those great beings of great supernatural power who practice the conduct of Brahmā are declared to be sages, the achievers of the state of heaven.
Those who are unattached to wandering through the realms of existence, whose faculties are well-stabilized,
and who practice the conduct of silence— they are remembered as sages.
Those who practice ascetic vows even without regard for their own bodies are declared to be true ascetics, seeking the noble glory of excellent virtues.
Those who are free from desire for the delights of illusion, who are undefiled, who have conquered their senses,
who are without the sense of "mine," self-restrained, and disciplined— those ascetics are stainless.

Those yogins who possess conduct based on universal faith, who are free from conceptual construction, who are without dependence, and whose selves are established in meditative absorption— they are stainless.
These practitioners of the vows of renunciation, liberated from existence,
with their very selves possessing purified faculties, shall attain the supreme goal.

How is it that you, who pride yourself on your learning and are arrogant with the intoxication of thinking "I shall conquer all," do not realize this even regarding such a very minor matter? Svp_200 //
Abandon pride, O master of the assembly; honor this one who has reached the further shore of the scriptures.
Practice for awakening, O seeker of liberation, and undertake the vow of renunciation.
Having said this, he related his own story in detail,
as well as the majestic power of the omniscient younger brother of Nalaka.
He alone is the lord of all vidyās in the three worlds, the wise one;
he is the lord of all dharmas, the Teacher who removes the pride of all disputants.
By the mere remembrance of whom my younger brother, that great sage,
became a conqueror of all disputants, a retainer of the Vedas, and one who has reached the further shore of learning.
What more need be said regarding the sight and hearing of such an omniscient one? Therefore, practice well-restrained conduct within his teaching.
Having heard these words in reply, that exceedingly audacious master of the assembly became joyful and resolute in his desire to undertake the vow of renunciation.
Having heard this instruction from the Teacher of the World,
the master of the gambling house, his soul deeply gladdened and awakened, offered his praise.
Then that wise master of the gambling hall, longing for the qualities of the Perfectly Awakened One,
bowed joyfully to the Lord of Munis and spoke thus with palms joined in reverence:
O Blessed One, omniscient one, wise one, who has reached the further shore of all knowledge,
O treasury of compassion, forgive my transgression which arose from my pride.
You alone are the Blessed One, the Protector, the Lord of all dharmas, the Victor;
you alone are the Teacher of the world, the Great Knower, the Sovereign of Sages.
The Tathāgata, the leader who has utterly conquered the four Māras,
you alone shine forth as the sovereign lord of the three realms.
O Blessed One, since I am eager to drink the nectar of the Dharma, [I seek] the sun of the knowledge of the true Dharma, which utterly destroys the darkness of the afflictions.
Therefore, having looked upon me, you ought to take heed:
I have always remained in the refuge of you, the Teacher.
Having received permission and composed myself, I shall practice for the state of the Sugata;
therefore, may you [grant it] regarding the Sugata’s Dharma, for the accomplishment of the Bodhisattva Bhadraśrī.
"Having united me with compassion, you ought to cause me to move about.
Having heard this prayer made by him, that ocean of compassion [responded].
Having observed that wandering mendicant Apamada, he spoke thus:
"Come, my good man; if you have a desire for the Saugata vow."
"Having undertaken the conduct of awakening, practice the vow free from afflictions"—
having thus instructed him, that Perfectly Awakened One himself [touched him] with his right hand.
Touching his head, he purified his threefold body;
when his head was touched by the Blessed One, he became shaven-headed and his senses were conquered.
The monk, clad in his robes, became a carrier of a vessel for thickened milk;
then, with a deeply serene mind, he received the permission of the Teacher of the World.
Having taken up the vow of the conduct of awakening, he practiced it with a concentrated mind;
then, his self purified by meditative absorption and the three spheres completely purified,
that ascetic follower of the Sugata became a celibate practitioner possessing great supernormal knowledge.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Practice of the Vows of Renunciation in the Saugata Teaching by the Lay Brother," in the *Śrī-Bhadrakalpāvadāna*, within the dialogue between Aśoka and Upagupta.
Having seen and heard this, even all the lords of the world rejoiced in that vow and proceeded forth, filled with delight.
Thus it was instructed by my teacher, and having heard it, I have spoken accordingly.
You too, O Great King, having heard this, should rejoice in it and practice it.
Having heard this, all those bodhisattvas with stainless faculties and great supernormal powers rejoice in me; may they become attainers of awakening.
Having heard what was thus taught by the Arhat in accordance with the scriptures, King Aśoka, filled with joy,
consented, saying "So be it," and rejoiced together with his retinue.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Practice of the Vows of Renunciation in the Teaching of the Sugata by the Master of the Assembly."
